analysis.one_liner: Restores federal pre-approval for state voting rule changes and expands voting access on tribal lands.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 48 senators, including one Republican, the bill never received a committee hearing or a floor vote and died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: After the Supreme Court's 2013 Shelby County decision struck down the old coverage formula, states no longer needed federal pre-approval before changing voting rules. This bill would rebuild that system on a new basis: any state or county with a recent record of voting rights violations — 15 violations in 25 years statewide, or 10 including one by the state itself — would have to get approval from the Justice Department or a federal court before putting in place certain voting changes, such as new voter ID requirements, closing or moving polling places, or redistricting that reduces minority voting strength. It would also require states to provide polling places and voter registration services on tribal lands when tribes request them, and to post public notices of voting changes and polling place resources.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters in states and counties with recent records of voting discrimination — especially Black, Latino, Asian American, and Native voters — gain a federal checkpoint before restrictive voting changes take effect. Tribal citizens gain guaranteed polling places, early voting locations, and registration services on Indian lands at no cost to tribes. Voters with disabilities gain public notices of voting changes in accessible formats.

how_it_helps.text: Restores the preclearance requirement — federal pre-approval before certain voting changes take effect — using a new formula that applies to states and counties with 15 or more voting rights violations in the past 25 years, or 10 or more including one committed by the state itself; covered jurisdictions include all of them for 10-year periods, with a path to bail out through a court judgment

Creates practice-based preclearance for specific changes regardless of where they happen: new or stricter voter ID requirements, adding at-large seats or reducing minority population shares in district boundaries, redistricting where a minority group grew by 10,000 people or 20%, cutting multilingual voting materials, and closing or relocating polling places in areas where a racial or language minority group is 20% of the voting-age population

Requires states, at no expense to tribes, to provide requested polling places on Indian lands, equal poll workers and voting equipment, early voting and absentee ballot locations, and to designate tribal offices as voter registration agencies

Requires state and local governments to post public notice, including online and in formats accessible to voters with disabilities, of changes to voting procedures within 48 hours and of the resources allocated to each polling place before federal elections

analysis.who_pays: State legislatures and local election offices in covered jurisdictions bear the cost of seeking federal approval for covered voting changes and of publicizing every change, and any state that has drawn a court objection in the past 25 years loses the ability to change voting rules without federal review. Critics argued the formula reaches far beyond the states the original 1965 law covered and can sweep in a state based on violations decades old.

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes a federal pre-approval process on covered states and counties, which can delay or block voting changes near an election: a covered practice cannot be implemented unless the Attorney General raises no objection within 60 days or a three-judge federal court approves it

The coverage formula is broad: a single state-level violation or a run of county-level violations spread over 25 years can put a whole state under preclearance, which critics said is a heavy burden on jurisdictions whose current practices may be lawful

The list of covered practices is wide — from redistricting to moving a polling place in any census tract where minority groups make up 20% of adults — so routine election administration decisions trigger federal review, adding compliance work for local election offices

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits run to the most fundamental interest ordinary voters have: the right to cast a ballot that counts, protected before a discriminatory rule takes effect rather than only after years of litigation. The costs fall on state and local election officials, not on voters, and the bill includes a bailout for jurisdictions with clean records and a 60-day approval path to keep routine changes moving. The strongest honest objection is that the formula's 25-year lookback can subject states to federal review long after their conduct has changed — a real cost, but one designed to be temporary and to end when a jurisdiction proves itself in court.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and died when the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Patrick Leahy introduced the bill on July 22, 2020, named for Rep. John Lewis, who had died four days earlier
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where no further action was ever taken on it
It carried the backing of 48 senators — 44 Democrats, 2 independents, and 1 Republican (Sen. Lisa Murkowski of Alaska) — a majority of the chamber
The Senate was controlled by Republicans, and the bill never reached the floor for any vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021

The bill sought to restore the preclearance system the Supreme Court invalidated in its 2013 Shelby County v. Holder decision, which struck down the Voting Rights Act's coverage formula and left states free to change election laws without federal pre-approval

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State legislatures and election officials — particularly in states with recent records of voting rights violations — remain free to change voting rules without federal pre-approval, and the post-2013 status quo, in which voting discrimination is addressed only through lawsuits after the fact, stayed in place. No one got a vote on the question.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: States facing no federal voting pre-approval

for.name: Civil rights organizations
for.what_they_did: Championed the legislation as the vehicle to restore the Voting Rights Act's protections after the 2013 Shelby County decision

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill, or any version of voting rights restoration, to the Senate floor for a vote during the 116th Congress

against.name: Lindsey Graham
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee hearing or markup after it was referred to his committee

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Held the chamber's majority and its agenda through the bill's entire five-month lifespan; only one Republican member of the caucus supported it

sides.party_line_note: Support was nearly unanimous among Senate Democrats and independents — 46 of 47 cosponsors — while exactly one Republican, Sen. Lisa Murkowski, joined; the Republican majority that controlled the Senate never acted on the bill.

industries.industry: State legislatures and election officials in jurisdictions with records of voting rights violations
industries.note: The bill would subject these officials to federal pre-approval before they could implement voting changes such as new ID rules, polling place closures, or redistricting plans. Its check on their discretion is the direct protection the bill offers voters, so their interest in blocking it ran against the voters it would cover.

industries.industry: State and local election administration generally
industries.note: The transparency provisions would require every state and larger locality to publicize voting changes and polling place resources within tight deadlines, adding compliance work. The same notices would give voters information about machine allocation and precinct changes that is now often opaque.
